advances: This proves a one-coordinate lift obstruction that permits singleton fibers. Under the precise old parity and reflection profile in the statement, the cardinality plus the number of singleton parity classes of a completed lift cannot exceed twice the old cardinality. Applied to the accepted twenty-point tetrahedron, it rules out every completed four-dimensional lift with reflection maximum at most three and cardinality plus singleton count greater than forty, without restricting the integer heights. The proof charges pairs that force two-point midpoint fibers against distinct old reflection-three centers. It does not classify equality, exclude arbitrary iterated singleton lifts, or resolve uniform-small-gain-separation or the locked weak Oertel conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The general inequality is proved by finite parity counts, the exact local table, and elementary convexity. Accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 supplies the concrete base and its verified reflection profile.
proof:
First count the old midpoint rows. In a lattice-convex set, any two distinct points of the same parity have an integer midpoint belonging to the set. Such an unordered pair contributes two nonzero oriented displacements at its midpoint. Together with the zero displacement, two different unordered pairs with the same midpoint would give reflection count at least five. Therefore every such pair has a reflection-three midpoint, different pairs have different midpoints, and every reflection-three point is the midpoint of exactly one such pair.

Let \(u_2\) and \(u_3\) be the numbers of occupied old parity classes of sizes two and three. Counting unordered distinct same-parity pairs gives \(u_2+3u_3\). Counting their distinct midpoint centers using the stated reflection profile gives \(2u_2+2u_3\). Consequently \(u_2=u_3\), and \(|B|=5u_2\).

For each \(x\in B\), write the actual fiber as \(I_x=\{t\in\mathbb Z:(x,t)\in A\}\). It is a nonempty consecutive integer interval, because it is the intersection of an interval in \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) with the integers. Write \(I_x=\{a_x,a_x+1,\ldots,a_x+L_x-1\}\). Each \(L_x\) lies in \(\{1,2,3,4\}\): five consecutive points would give the zero displacement and the four vertical displacements of lengths one and two at the third point of that fiber. This argument includes every additional lattice point that taking the convex hull might have produced.

Take distinct \(x,y\in B\) of the same parity. Suppose that \(L_x,L_y\ge2\). If \(a_x+a_y\) were odd, the two unordered endpoint pairs
\(\{(x,a_x),(y,a_y+1)\}\) and \(\{(x,a_x+1),(y,a_y)\}\) would have the same integer center. That center belongs to \(A\) by lattice-convexity, so the pairs and zero displacement would give reflection count at least five. Thus \(a_x+a_y\) is even. If \(L_x\ge3\), apply the same argument to the two-point subintervals with lower endpoints \(a_x+1\) and \(a_y\), whose sum is odd. This is impossible. Interchanging \(x,y\) gives \(L_x=L_y=2\).

For any old same-parity pair \(x,y\), consider the integer last-coordinate heights of midpoints of one lifted point over \(x\) and one over \(y\). There cannot be two distinct endpoint pairs at one integer center, by the preceding reflection argument. The permitted fiber lengths now give the following complete description of when there are two integer midpoint heights: both lengths are two; one length is four and the other is one; or one length is three and the other is one with \(a_x+a_y\) even. In each of these cases the two heights are consecutive integers. All other permitted cases have at most one integer midpoint height.

For clarity, the description follows directly by adding the height intervals. When both lengths are two, the lower endpoints have equal parity, and the two even endpoint sums are \(a_x+a_y\) and \(a_x+a_y+2\). When one fiber has size one, the sums form a consecutive integer interval with exactly as many members as the other fiber. Four such sums have exactly two even members; three have two even members exactly when the first sum is even; one or two sums have at most one even member.

Whenever an old pair produces two integer midpoint heights \(c,c+1\), its old midpoint \(j=(x+y)/2\) has exactly the two-point fiber \(I_j=\{c,c+1\}\). Indeed, both points belong to \(A\) by lattice-convexity and each already has a reflected pair with distinct old base endpoints. If \(I_j\) extended below \(c\), its consecutiveness would provide the additional vertical reflected pair at height \(c\) with endpoints \(c-1,c+1\). If it extended above \(c+1\), it would provide the analogous vertical pair at height \(c+1\). Either case would give reflection count at least five. The old midpoint \(j\) has reflection count three in \(B\).

For each occupied parity class \(C\) of \(B\), define three local counts. Let \(q(C)\) be the number of lifted points over \(C\), plus the number of its two last-coordinate parity refinements that are singletons. Let \(t(C)\) be the number of points \(x\in C\) with \(r_B(x)=3\) and \(L_x=2\). Let \(f(C)\) be the number of unordered distinct pairs in \(C\) that produce two integer midpoint heights as just described. Thus \(\sum_C q(C)=|A|+s(A)\). Each pair counted by some \(f(C)\) forces a two-point fiber at its old reflection-three midpoint. Different old pairs have different midpoints. Hence \(\sum_C f(C)\le\sum_C t(C)\).

The following local inequalities contain the remaining argument: \(2q(C)+t(C)-f(C)\le9\) when \(|C|=2\), and \(2q(C)+t(C)-f(C)\le11\) when \(|C|=3\). Here is the complete case table. Within the table, \(q,t,f\) denote the three counts for its one class, and the fiber lengths are listed as an unordered multiset.

| Class size | Fiber lengths | Possible \(q\) | Bound on \(t\) | Value or condition for \(f\) | Maximum \(2q+t-f\) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | \((1,1)\) | 2 or 4 | 0 | 0 | 8 |
| 2 | \((1,2)\) | 4 | 1 | 0 | 9 |
| 2 | \((1,3)\) | 4 or 5 | 0 | 1 if \(q=5\), otherwise 0 | 9 |
| 2 | \((1,4)\) | 5 | 0 | 1 | 9 |
| 2 | \((2,2)\) | 4 | 2 | 1 | 9 |
| 3 | \((1,1,1)\) | 3 or 4 | 0 | 0 | 8 |
| 3 | \((1,1,2)\) | 4 or 5 | at most 1 | 0 | 11 |
| 3 | \((1,1,3)\) | 5 or 6 | 0 | 2 if \(q=6\), otherwise 0 or 1 | 10 |
| 3 | \((1,1,4)\) | 6 | 0 | 2 | 10 |
| 3 | \((1,2,2)\) | 5 | at most 2 | 1 | 11 |
| 3 | \((2,2,2)\) | 6 | 2 | 3 | 11 |

The table is exhaustive because two nonsingleton fibers in one old parity class must both have length two. Thus a fiber of length three or four forces every other fiber in that class to be a singleton; otherwise all lengths are one or two. To verify the \(q\) column, split the total points between even and odd last coordinates, and add one for each split part of size one. For example, lengths \((1,3)\) give split sizes \((3,1)\) or \((2,2)\), whereas lengths \((1,1,3)\) give \((4,1)\) or \((3,2)\), up to order. A two-point fiber supplies one point of each parity, and a four-point fiber supplies two of each parity. These observations give every other displayed \(q\) value directly.

The two conditional \(f\) entries follow from the same parity calculation. A three-point fiber has two points of its lower-endpoint parity and one of the other parity. For lengths \((1,3)\), the contribution is five exactly when the singleton has the lower-endpoint parity of the three-point fiber. That pair then produces two integer midpoint heights. For lengths \((1,1,3)\), the contribution is six exactly when both singletons have that lower-endpoint parity; both corresponding pairs then produce two integer midpoint heights. If the contribution is five, at most one singleton has that parity. Every other \(f\) entry follows from the complete midpoint-height description above. Finally, both members of a size-two class have old reflection count three, while a size-three class has only two such members. This explains the \(t\) bounds, including \(t=2\) for three length-two fibers. The last column follows by substitution, proving the local inequalities.

Summing them, using \(u_2=u_3\) and the fact that a midpoint is charged at most once, gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(|A|+s(A)\bigr)
&\le 2\sum_C q(C)+\sum_C\bigl(t(C)-f(C)\bigr)\\
&\le 9u_2+11u_3
=20u_2
=4|B|.
\end{aligned}
\]

This proves \(|A|+s(A)\le2|B|\). The argument used the actual integer intervals and necessary restrictions on every old same-parity pair. It neither bounds the lower endpoints nor identifies a supplied generator list with a completed lattice set.

For the concrete consumer, accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 gives the full twenty-point census \(p_0,\ldots,p_{19}\) of \(B_3\). Its size-two parity classes are \(\{p_6,p_{16}\}\), \(\{p_{11},p_{14}\}\), \(\{p_{10},p_{17}\}\), and \(\{p_3,p_7\}\). Its size-three classes are \(\{p_0,p_{12},p_{18}\}\), \(\{p_2,p_5,p_8\}\), \(\{p_1,p_4,p_{15}\}\), and \(\{p_9,p_{13},p_{19}\}\). The same fact verifies reflection count one exactly at \(p_0,p_1,p_2,p_{19}\), and reflection count three at every other point. Thus the size-two classes consist of reflection-three points and each size-three class contains exactly one reflection-one point. For this particular base the four reflection-one points are also exactly the vertices, as that fact verifies; the general theorem did not require that identification. The theorem therefore applies with \(|B_3|=20\).

To check sharpness directly, the convex hull of \(B_3\times\{0,1\}\) is \(P\times[0,1]\), whose integer points are exactly \(B_3\times\{0,1\}\). Its dimension is four because \(P\) has dimension three. At a supported center, any integer displacement in the last coordinate must be zero, since both reflected last coordinates lie in \(\{0,1\}\). The reflection count is therefore the old reflection count, and its maximum is three. A center outside the support has reflection count zero by lattice-convexity. Each occupied old parity class splits into two new parity classes of the same old size, so there are eight new classes of size two and eight of size three, with no singleton class. Its forty actual lattice points consequently attain \(|A|+s(A)=40\).

The theorem permits the equality case without determining its parity profile. A later arbitrary lift can use this result again only after its new base is shown to satisfy the same hypotheses. In particular, the present proof leaves open whether a sharp lift of this tetrahedron can have singleton parity classes and supply a different base for further lifting.
statement:
For a finite set \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^m\), use the canonical oriented, zero-inclusive reflection count \(r_X(j)=|\{v\in\mathbb Z^m:j+v,j-v\in X\}|\), for \(j\in\mathbb Z^m\). Let \(s(X)\) be the number of ambient parity classes modulo \(2\mathbb Z^m\) containing exactly one point of \(X\).

Let \(n\ge1\), and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be a nonempty finite lattice-convex set with \(\max_j r_B(j)\le3\). Assume that every occupied parity class of \(B\) has size two or three, every point of a size-two class has reflection count three, and each size-three class contains exactly one point with reflection count one and two points with reflection count three. These are hypotheses about reflection counts; reflection-one points are not assumed to coincide with geometric vertices.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^{n+1}\) be any nonempty finite lattice-convex set whose projection onto the first \(n\) coordinates is exactly \(B\), and suppose \(\max_j r_A(j)\le3\). Then \(|A|+s(A)\le2|B|\). No lower bound greater than one is imposed on a nonempty fiber, and no bound is imposed on its location in the last coordinate. The fibers in this assertion are all actual fibers of \(A=\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^{n+1}\).

For the concrete consumer, let \(B_3\) denote the support called \(A\) in accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7, namely \(B_3=P\cap\mathbb Z^3\), where \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(31,53,78)\}\). Every lift of \(B_3\) satisfying the preceding hypotheses obeys \(|A|+s(A)\le40\). This bound is sharp: \(B_3\times\{0,1\}\) is full-dimensional and lattice-convex in \(\mathbb Z^4\), has forty points, has no singleton parity class, and has reflection maximum three.
